The palette is deliberate and unusual, shifting between dusty pink, violet dusk, sky blue, sage and deep green.
The lighting changes from shot to shot: backlit glass, a volcanic glow, studio softbox and translucent subsurface. Each frame works as a poster.
The studio-name credits (Boldtron, Medusa Lab) and a custom OFFF MX lockup point to a festival collaborative-titles format by real studios.
The landscapes recur across shots, so the sequence implies a journey through one world.
gaps: The idea is the familiar festival format of 'organic-surreal 3D creatures'. It needs a concept as specific as B's clockwork map or C's cigarette packs.
The typography is small default bold-sans studio labels pasted top-left. Integrating the type into the world would fix this.
The connective narrative between the studio segments is weak. Choreography that carries forms from shot to shot would make it one film rather than a reel.

defects: No busy-moment strips were supplied, so I judged spacing and easing only from the paired frames. The paired frames show mostly rigid translation: the stacked 'Offset' layers and the ticker rows slide as solid blocks, with no visible overlap, squash or follow-through.
Dead air at the end: change per second falls to 11.4, 5.9, 2.7 and 12.4 over the last ~4 s. The final lockup holds almost static, and the motion is mostly the RGB fringe settling.

The ticker section (frames 3-4) is a stock marquee pattern: rows of 'OFFSET' scrolling in alternating directions. It is the busiest part of the film but also the most template-like, and the rows clip the word at the frame edges with no considered crop.

The RGB/CMY fringe is applied at the same amount everywhere, including the small metadata type ('Design Systems Conference', '14–15 May 2027'). At 100% it softens the counters and gives magenta/green halos on black text.
The italic serif tagline 'One system, every offset.' is tiny and low-contrast against the blue, and it introduces a second type family that has no other role in the film.
Frame 2 (the CMYK overprint stack) is busy: the four overlapping layers make the word hard to read, and the dark navy layer muddies the overprint rather than mixing like ink.
The middle shot runs 5.9 s, and the energy plateaus from ~5 s to ~10 s instead of building to a single peak.
gaps: Choreography: the misregistration idea is shown with linear block slides and a scrolling marquee. Top studios would make the plates behave like physical print: registration snapping in with weight, ink layers overshooting and settling, overlapping offsets between plates. The film also needs a single clear peak at ~70% before the lockup.

Sound: the structure is reasonable (sparse ticks, a noise riser to a drop at ~6 s, dense hits, then a sparse tail with a final hit at 14.1 s). But the bed reads as broadband noise plus simple tonal partials, with little mid-range texture or sound design tied to the print idea (press clatter, paper, registration clicks), and the drop is a generic riser.

Finish and ending: the uniform chromatic-aberration filter is laid over everything instead of being a real plate offset with ink overprint. It degrades small text. The end card is static for ~3 s with only a fringe settle, and the lockup's second typeface and tiny tagline weaken the payoff.
